title: What makes us human
takeaway: Being human means keeping your promises, living with purpose, and being one heart with others.
scene: This ghazal is printed in two columns. It begins almost like a lesson about what makes a good person, then turns into a love poem.

original: کسے نال پیار دا پیمان ہونا
دلاں دا دوستو اک جان ہونا
transliteration: Kise naal pyaar da paimaan hona
Dilaan da dosto ik jaan hona
translation: Having a promise of love with someone,
couplets.story: To make a real promise of love to someone, so that two hearts become like one soul...

translation: A person being noble in what they do:
this is what it means to be human.
couplets.story: ...and to be a person whose actions are good and honourable. That, he says, is what being human really means.

original: اوہ سانوں موت دے مونہہ لے گیا اے
کسے لئی جین دا ارمان ہونا
transliteration: Oh saanu maut de moonh lai gaya ae
Kise layi jeen da armaan hona
translation: It has carried me into the jaws of death:
wanting to live for someone else.
couplets.story: Wanting to live for someone else has put him right in danger. Love is risky.

original: روگاں درد دے دتے پرا گے
جویں جثے دا ہے بے جان ہونا
transliteration: Jiven jusse da hai be-jaan hona
translation: The pains and illnesses of love have left me
like a body with the life drained out of it.
couplets.story: All the pain of love has left him feeling like an empty body with no life left in it.

original: اوہ شیشے ساہمنے نے آ کھلوتے
کسے دی موت دا سامان ہونا
transliteration: Oh sheeshe saahmne ne aa khalote
Kise di maut da saamaan hona
translation: The beloved came and stood in front of the mirror:
that's enough to be the death of someone.
couplets.story: The Beloved stands in front of a mirror, and that sight alone is enough to make someone's heart stop.

original: کرم دی جھات ایسی پے گئی اے
کہ درداں سکھ لیا درمان ہونا
transliteration: Karam di jhaat aisi pai gayi ae
Ke dardaan sikh liya darmaan hona
translation: Such a glance of kindness has fallen on me
that my pains have learned to become the cure.
couplets.story: Then one kind look from the Beloved changes everything. Suddenly his pain itself starts to heal him.

original: دلاں دے شہر کر تسخیر جاندا
ایہہ تیرے حسن دا سلطان ہونا
transliteration: Dilaan de shehar kar taskheer jaanda
Eh tere husn da sultaan hona
translation: It goes about conquering whole cities of hearts:
this is your beauty being king.
couplets.story: The Beloved's beauty is like a king that conquers whole cities of hearts.

original: مینوں کفیر کہہ کے رکھ چھڈ نا احمدؔ
نئیں دلبر دا جد تک آن ہونا
transliteration: Mainu kaafir keh ke rakh chhadna Ahmad
Nahin dilbar da jad tak aan hona
translation: Ahmad, they'll keep calling me an unbeliever
couplets.story: He ends by saying people will keep calling him an 'unbeliever' for loving the way he does, at least until the Beloved finally arrives and proves him right.

deeper:
The opening couplets are almost a definition of the Sufi ideal of a human being. That person keeps faith in love, is one heart with others, and is noble in action.

After one glance of grace, 'my pains have learned to become the cure'. The pain is the same, but how he sees it has changed. For Sufis, that change in seeing is the real transformation: God's kindness turns suffering into healing.

Being called a 'kafir' (unbeliever) for loving too much is a bold image used by Bulleh Shah and others. Strict, narrow people sometimes condemned the mystics' passionate love for God. The poet says that judgment will stand until the Beloved Himself appears.
why: It starts with a definition of a good human being that anyone can relate to, before becoming a love poem.
prompt: What do you think makes someone truly 'human'?
notes: Printed in two columns; read here as a ghazal with the right-hand line first. The first two rows read as one continuous thought.
